I got **capy-flash running natively on Windows** with 2× RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB, a Ryzen 7 9800X3D, and 128 GB DDR5.

The biggest issue was the \~64.6 GiB routed-expert bank. The original approach used a large pinned, CUDA-mapped host allocation so the GPUs could read expert weights directly over PCIe. On my Windows/CUDA 13.4 setup, host registration and GPU mapping repeatedly failed with `cudaErrorMemoryAllocation`, even when registering the memory in separate 1 GiB chunks.

The fix was to change the Windows Offload path to keep the full expert bank in **ordinary pageable system RAM**, rather than trying to pin and map the entire bank. When an expert needs to be loaded into the GPU cache, the code copies its data into a bounded pinned-memory bounce buffer and then performs the asynchronous host-to-device transfer. Each buffer stays alive until its CUDA completion event finishes. I also guarded against the optional unstaged miss-split path, which would otherwise attempt direct GPU reads from the pageable bank. The original HostMapped behavior remains available for the Mapped backend.

There were a few additional Windows portability fixes, including replacing `gmtime_r`, fixing a `DevicePlacement` initializer, and correcting some `fprintf` argument mismatches.

**Current result:** the native server builds, completes startup and CUDA graph warmup, and successfully handles real chat-completion requests. The logs showed 69.6 GiB of artifact data read but only 6.51 GiB of weights uploaded to the GPUs, with the expert bank remaining host-resident. I measured about 28.5 generated tokens/sec on one request with MTP enabled.

It still needs longer stability and performance testing, and VRAM headroom is tight on the GPU driving my displays. But the key lesson was that keeping all experts in host RAM doesn't require making the entire bank directly GPU-addressable: pageable storage plus bounded pinned staging was the way around the Windows registration bottleneck.

Thanks, this is the first native Windows run of Flash-Next we know of, and the pageable bank + bounded pinned staging is the right way around WDDM's pinning limits. The speculative decoding has to be done on the same highest probability token distribution than the main model is.

Otherwise it's speculation can change the quality. Consider this:

Main model distribution for next token:
1. tok1 (chosen p=20%)
2. tok2 (chosen 20%)
3. tok3 (chosen 20%)
4. tok4 (chosen 20%)
5. tok5 (chosen 20%)

Draft speculates with different distribution and gets
1. tok1 (chosen p=25%)
2. tok3 (chosen 25%)
3. tok6 (chosen 25%)
4. tok7 (chosen 25%)

And draft picks tok3 and main model accepts it, but as the probabilities is not the same for all tokens, the draft skews main model output.

I’m running Qwen 3.8 27B on an array of 12 TITAN Vs (2 e5-2696 v3 and 1TB DDR4) using a custom llama.cpp back-end I coded with help from Claude.  It serves the model lossless: lossless BF16 weights, 22bit KV up to 512K contexts compressing into a 12bit history form (used in addition to a long 22bit tail) for contexts up to 1M.  It serves up to 8 slots concurrently when all the contexts fit.  I currently get about 50 t/s single stream decode, over 100 t/s concurrent decode (rarely) and about 5000 t/s prefill.  The performance numbers are provisional because Claude is currently working through a list of performance optimisations (prefill doubled today for example).  I chose the quantisation against a double precision reference implementation and 1/2 ULP perturbation of the BF16 weights such that the model is served with accuracy well within the precision of its weights and I believe the probability of a token flip compared to the double precision reference is about 1 in 300000. I.e aiming at a reference implementation of the model.  I’ve done a little work using it for Opencode and to review its own back-end source code in runs that have lasted up to 10 hours and it seems to work quite well.
